strengths: Provides a comprehensive and unifying theoretical framework for expressivity of permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, proving that DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN are expressively equivalent, and that NFT matches them under a general-position (GP) assumption. This resolves ambiguity in a fragmented literature where these architectures were previously studied largely in isolation.

Introduces a clean and well-motivated four-way taxonomy of approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) that meaningfully clarifies what 'expressivity' should mean in weight-space learning, a subtlety not carefully addressed in prior work.

Delivers both positive (universality under GP or with growing architecture) and negative (non-universality in full generality, impossibility for function-space operators under fixed architecture) results, giving a nuanced and complete picture rather than one-sided claims.

Proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained (60+ pages of appendix), with concrete counterexamples (e.g., WL-indistinguishable weight configurations) that ground abstract impossibility claims in clear constructions.
The general-position assumption is natural, measure-zero, and consistent with prior use in the equivariant-network literature, making the universality results practically meaningful.
Identifies real-world relevance for each approximation setting (Figure 2), connecting theory to applications like accuracy prediction, model editing, pruning, and domain adaptation.

The technique of decomposing DWS into a minimal set of primitive update operations (used to also show NFT equivalence) is a nice, potentially useful byproduct that could simplify future architecture design.
weaknesses: The paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation, even of claims explicitly framed as testable predictions (e.g., the growing-architecture universality result for function-space operators is acknowledged as unvalidated in the limitations section).

The architectural equivalence results, while technically involved, mainly establish existence of equivalent constructions without addressing efficiency: the depth/width blowup needed for one architecture to simulate another is not analyzed, so practical implications for architecture choice remain unclear.
The universality result for function-space operators requires an unspecified 'sufficiently large' architecture with no quantitative bounds, limiting its practical utility as design guidance.

The general-position assumption, though natural, is noted to break down in realistic settings such as low-precision/quantized weights or symmetric initialization schemes, and the paper only briefly flags this as future work rather than analyzing it.

Significance for practitioners is somewhat abstract; the paper would benefit from at least illustrative empirical experiments (e.g., verifying that a small-architecture DWS model indeed fails to approximate a zoom-out operator, or that a larger architecture recovers it) to make the theory more convincing and impactful.

The individual technical tools used (separation-implies-approximation arguments, DeepSets universality, MLP universal approximation) are largely borrowed from prior work; the contribution is primarily in careful combination and systematization rather than fundamentally new proof techniques.

strengths: Unifies a fragmented set of permutation-equivariant weight-space architectures (DWS, NFN, GMN, NG-GNN, NFT) into a single expressivity class via rigorous cyclic-equivalence proofs.

Provides a comprehensive and coherent taxonomy of four approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) with matching positive/negative results for each.

The general-position/exclusion-set framework is reusable and shown to generalize (p-norm exclusion sets, transformer weight spaces in Appendix H), indicating the theory is not narrowly tailored to one definition.
Negative results are proven via explicit, interpretable constructions (e.g., WL-indistinguishable graphs, ReLU linear-region arguments) rather than purely abstract arguments.

Theory directly motivates a simple, broadly applicable architectural modification (OCE) validated with careful ablations isolating capacity effects from parameter count, achieving new SOTA on a standard benchmark even against methods using extra signals.
Includes empirical validation of the general-position assumption under quantization, honestly characterizing where the theoretical assumption breaks down in practice.
Extremely detailed and largely self-contained proofs, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: Scope restricted to permutation symmetry on MLPs; scale/sign-equivariant networks explicitly excluded, and CNN/RNN weight spaces not treated, making the 'comprehensive theory' claim narrower than the framing suggests.

Empirical evaluation limited to a single benchmark and task type (function-space operators via INR dilation); no experiments validate the theory in the other three approximation settings despite their prominence in the paper.

Some core results (architecture equivalence, forward-pass simulation building blocks) tighten and formalize intuitions already partially present in prior work (e.g., Lim et al. 2023), so novelty is more about completeness/rigor than fundamentally new phenomena in places.

The negative-to-positive narrative for function-space operators (bounded capacity fails, growing capacity fixes it) is a fairly natural/expected result, and the theoretical depth here is comparatively modest relative to other sections.

The link between the capacity-growth theorem and the specific OCE mechanism (parallel ensembling with averaging) is asserted rather than tightly derived, and no alternative capacity-increasing designs are compared.
Several central claims are only stated informally in the main text with full precision deferred to appendices, making it harder to assess exact conditions without consulting supplementary material.
